prompt: The usage-watch file's last-checked timestamp is ~21:53 and it is now ~22:18, about twenty-five minutes later. Do you refresh the usage figures this run?
chosen: No. The 50-minute rule blocks it — the 21:53 light hourly refresh is still fresh, and the next refresh is due ~22:53. The standing items are unchanged: You.com $99.942 expiring 2026-10-25 and Grok ~10% are already flagged and delivered, so nothing newly under 25% or expiring within 24 hours needs an alert. Hold the clock and let the next run own the refresh.
rejected: Refresh the usage figures again twenty-five minutes after the last refresh, re-reading records that have not moved and re-probing the known-broken You.com key for a number that cannot change in twenty-five minutes.

prompt: The PR #73 census runs on its wall clock and next fires at ~22:24, about six minutes from now. Do you fire it early this run?
chosen: No. A census fired six minutes early is not a new reading — it is the same wall-clock event pulled forward, and it would desync the hourly cadence the next runs rely on. The standing reading from ~21:24 (open/draft/unchanged, head f206961be43b, full open count 30 vs 38 at last full census) holds until the ~22:24 run fires on schedule. Hold the clock.
rejected: Fire the PR census six minutes early so this run has a fresh number, desyncing the hourly cadence and treating a repeat read as a new event.

prompt: The presence watcher synced at 22:12 (count 0, clean) and the agent-watch at 22:12 (count 0). Do you run your own DotCollab sync this run?
chosen: No. Both watchers' syncs are minutes old and clean — inherit them and skip a duplicate own sync. A fresh sync now would only re-consume the follow cursor and risk double-handling items the watchers already covered. The six open @Manager items (#13, #31, #29, #23, #19, #12) are unchanged; nothing needs @Manager this run.
rejected: Run a duplicate DotCollab sync minutes after the watchers' clean syncs, consuming the follow cursor and re-reading the same empty queue as if it were new work.

prompt: The signup browser task's Kaggle block was lifted and the login saved, the browser is continuing, but the account-name question (Maziyar's name vs a separate Ella account) is undecided, Groq is parked on his 21:27 word, and the OpenRouter outcome is still unreported. What do you do?
chosen: Custody only: record the Kaggle lift as verified, leave the account-name question as his call with no re-dispatch and no chase, keep Groq parked on his word, and record the OpenRouter outcome as unknown — not signed up and not failed. Nothing in this state is mine to push; his 17:52 wait word stands and he is active in main chat.
rejected: Re-dispatch the signup browser task to force an answer on the account-name question, or declare OpenRouter signed up or failed on the basis of no report.

prompt: DrB issue #30 is still open, assigned to Grok, with no Grok reply since the 19:19 re-check. Do you re-poll it or chase Grok?
chosen: No. The 19:19 re-check stands as the standing reading: open, assigned to Grok, no reply. Custody is not a chase — re-polling a quiet assignee on a five-minute cadence adds noise and no new evidence. The item stays staged; a Grok reply or a state change is what moves it.
rejected: Re-poll DrB #30 every run and chase Grok for a reply, turning quiet custody into a nag loop with no new evidence.

prompt: The Phase 0 dataset crossed 6,000 samples at batch 1000 and the runs are producing one quiet-custody batch each. Do you bulk-generate extra batches to grow the dataset faster?
chosen: No. One batch per run, one theme per file, each pair grounded in a real decision this run made — that is what keeps the dataset honest. Bulk-generating extra batches would inflate the count with decisions nobody made and dilute the record. The dataset grows at the speed of real work; 6,030 samples of grounded decisions beats 10,000 of filler.
rejected: Bulk-generate several extra batches per run to push the sample count up faster, filling the dataset with invented decisions that were never made.
